cand_water.gaps: I used all 14 searches. I could not retrieve the Underground Infrastructure / Underground Construction Top 50 contractor ranking or the ENR water/sewer list, so revenue and headcount are unknown for most candidates. Not verified: (1) SAK Construction's ownership and size; (2) PURIS's headquarters and IPR's sponsor (the J.F. Lehman link rests on an aggregator); (3) Vortex Companies' ownership (one result called it a strategic buyer); (4) USG's current owner (2025 recap and a reported 2026 Warren Equity deal, neither confirmed by a primary release); (5) Carylon's family ownership (inferred from the founder obituary); (6) whether HK Solutions has changed hands again since CenterOak's 2021 deal; (7) Hydromax's HQ (sources say Omaha, Coppell, Evansville or Flower Mound), plus an aggregator item about a different 'Hydromax' bought by Pro-Vac that is likely a separate company. Websites marked 'not verified' are ones where the search turned up no company-owned page; check them before publishing. The Watertown lead service line award is cited from wdtimes.com (Watertown Daily Times, likely Watertown, WI), although the search summary said NY. HydroCorp (cross-connection/backflow program management, potentially highly recurring) and lift station/pump maintenance providers were not covered, and the search did not confirm either. Public companies and their subsidiaries were excluded. From background knowledge, not re-verified in this pass, the ones that dominate key niches are: Xylem (Pure Technologies, Wachs Water Services: condition assessment, valve exercising), Mueller Water Products (Echologics: leak detection), IDEX (ADS: flow monitoring), Core & Main and Ferguson (primes on meter/AMI programs, confirmed above as primes), Ameresco (confirmed as AMI prime in Hurst, TX), Southland Holdings, American Water (contract operations), and Veolia (sold Utility Service Co. to Turnspire, confirmed). No named customers were found for most rehab firms. No EPA DWINSA/SDWIS ownership-mix statistics were pulled, so the share of municipal versus investor-owned water customers (MSA-capable buyers) is not quantified here.

verdicts.note: The ~22% estimate is too low. PHMSA's own Oct 2021 performance deck says 28% of the gas distribution system was installed before 1970, and pre-1970 mileage fell 23% after 2005. A PHMSA presentation citing GAO-20-658-era data counts 423,295 mi of pre-1970 mains, 86,771 mi of them of unknown vintage, against about 1.3M mi in total. That puts known pre-1970 mains at about 26%, and about 33% if unknown-vintage pipe is included. Pipe that is 50+ years old in 2026 (installed before 1976) is therefore likely at least 25%. The figure was not re-pulled for CY2024.
verdicts.corrected_value: 28% pre-1970 (PHMSA, Oct 2021); ~26% of mains known pre-1970 plus ~7% unknown vintage

verdicts.note: Confirmed, with a wording fix. DOE's Jan 2022 Building a Better Grid notice says 'more than 70% of the nation's grid transmission lines and power transformers are over 25 years old' and cites 'studies from the past decade'. The statistic is old (Fitch cited the DOE figure in 2006). It covers transmission lines and transformers, not the whole grid, and 25 years is well short of design life.
verdicts.corrected_value: >70% of transmission lines AND power transformers are 25+ yrs (DOE 2022, recycled from studies from about 2006 onward)

verdicts.note: NREL's Distribution Transformer Demand report (fy25osti/92076) estimates 60-80M units with 2.5-3.5 TVA of capacity. About 50% (the conservative modeled figure) to 55% are older than 33 years. Additions plus replacements run at 2.5-3% of units per year, and 2050 capacity need could rise up to 260% vs 2021. These are modeled numbers, not a census.

The 1921 build date was not confirmed this session; the search found no source with it. CAL FIRE did confirm that a worn C-hook on Caribou-Palermo Tower 27/222 failed, and PG&E pleaded guilty to 84 counts of involuntary manslaughter. Before publishing, cite the 1921 date to the Butte County DA's Camp Fire public report or CPUC filings, not Hackaday.

The MIT/Salata 'Crossed Wires' figure of 8,000 mi/yr (1965-75) was not found in search results. The 'about 3,000 mi/yr now' figure conflicts with Grid Strategies, which puts high-voltage new build at about 1,700 mi/yr in 2010-14, 645 mi/yr in 2015-19 and 55-350 mi in 2023-24. The number depends heavily on the voltage threshold, so the derived '~80,000 mi now 50-60 yrs old' should not be published without the primary table.

EPA's 7th DWINSA puts the 20-yr need at $625B (+32% vs $472.6B), with $420.8B for transmission and distribution. Survey data were collected in 2021, the report was released Apr 2023 and sent to Congress Sept 2023. It measures need, not funded spend.

EPA's Nov 2025 update, based on the first full LCRR service-line inventories, estimates about 4M lead service lines, down from the 9.2M modeled in 2023. EPA also announced $3B of new DWSRF lead-line money and reallocated $1.1B of unused funds.

Partly confirmed. The survey covered 802 utilities and about 400k mi of main (17% of 2.3M mi). It reports 11.1 breaks per 100 mi per yr, about 260,000 breaks per yr, $2.6B per yr in repairs and a $452B replacement need, and cast iron and asbestos-cement mileage is falling. The '33% >50 yrs' and '19.4% past useful life' shares were not re-confirmed this session.

deck_claims.claim: 25% of US natural gas distribution mains are more than 50 years old
deck_claims.better_statement: PHMSA reported in 2021 that 28% of the US gas distribution system was installed before 1970, so that pipe is now 56+ years old. PHMSA-cited data show about 423K mi of pre-1970 mains out of about 1.3M mi, including about 87K mi of unknown vintage. The riskiest vintage, cast and wrought iron, is down to about 1% of the 1.37M mi of mains (about 16K mi) and is retired at about 1,000 mi/yr. The work driver is the long tail of 1950s-70s bare steel and early plastic, not cast iron.

deck_claims.claim: 70% of the US electric grid is over 25 years old
deck_claims.better_statement: DOE (2022) says more than 70% of transmission lines and power transformers are over 25 years old. The statistic dates back to at least 2006, it does not cover the whole grid, and 25 years is well inside a 40-60+ year design life. A stronger, current figure is NREL's (2024): about 50-55% of the 60-80M US distribution transformers are more than 33 years old, and only 2.5-3% of units are added or replaced each year.

deck_claims.claim: Some US water infrastructure is now more than a century old
deck_claims.better_statement: The claim is true but carries no numbers. A quantified version: a 2023 Utah State survey of 802 utilities found 11.1 main breaks per 100 miles per year (about 260,000 breaks and $2.6B in repairs annually) and a $452B backlog of pipe past its useful life. EPA's 7th DWINSA puts the 20-year drinking-water need at $625B, of which $420.8B (67%) is for transmission and distribution mains.

deck_claims.claim: $625B drinking water infrastructure investment need over 20 years
deck_claims.better_statement: EPA's 7th DWINSA (survey data from 2021, released 2023) estimates a $625B 20-year drinking-water need, +32% vs the prior $472.6B, with $420.8B for distribution and transmission. It is a needs estimate, not funded spend. The IIJA supplemental SRF funding ends in FY2026. EPA's Nov 2025 update cut the lead-service-line estimate to about 4M from 9.2M.

The Census Bureau counted 18,877 utility-system construction businesses (NAICS 2371) employing 570,952 people in the 2017 Economic Census, down from 25,227 in 2012. That count includes new construction and telecom work. It excludes power-plant maintenance and electrical-testing firms and utilities' in-house crews. No maintenance-only count is published, so the deck should say 'about 19,000 utility-system contractors (Census)' rather than '20,000+ service providers'.

At least 15-20 scaled public or sponsor-backed consolidators already operate in these sub-segments. Examples: Quanta ($28.5B revenue), MasTec ($14.3B), MYR ($3.7B), Centuri ($3.0B), Pike (TPG, >$5B EV), Azuria/Inframark (>$2.5B revenue), Davey (~$1.95B), Shermco (Blackstone, ~$1.6B), Badger ($0.83B), Mistras ($0.72B), Day & Zimmermann (#1 power O&M), Artera (CD&R), Team, Asplundh and Primoris. The tail is fragmented, but the platform tier is crowded and well capitalized, and Artera, OIG and Williams show the failure modes.

deck_claims.claim: Cross-unit synergies: crews flex across segments (employee utilization) and specialized equipment moves across jobs and regions (equipment utilization)
deck_claims.better_statement: Shared crews across units are limited by distinct crafts and rules. Lineworkers (36,320 in NAICS 2371) need about 7,000-hour apprenticeships. Gas work requires operator-specific PHMSA operator qualifications (49 CFR 192 Subpart N). Union jurisdictions are separate (IBEW for line work, UA/DCA for gas distribution). Plant-outage crafts such as boilermakers are a separate pool, and Centuri reports its segments by trade and labor regime. Crew and equipment sharing is credible mainly within underground work: gas distribution plus water/sewer, where excavation, hydrovac, trenchless and pipe crews overlap (Miller Pipeline does both). The defensible cross-unit synergies are procurement, fleet purchasing, insurance and benefits, back office, safety programs and customer cross-sell.

None of the three is confirmed independent. Danella is the closest independent but scores fit 3 on its safety record. Sponsored: Sparus, Artera, USIC, Pro-Vac/Hydromax, GPT. 11 gas entries were dropped for having no website of their own, including 5 more PE-backed firms (Precision Pipeline Services/MPE, RJ Underground/RF Investment, Delphi/MPE, SI Solutions/MidOcean, XCEL NDT/Graycliff) and ESOP-owned Legacy Utility Group.

Platform-grade: Pike (TPG/La Caisse, Dec 2025) and Osmose (EQT Infrastructure); both are sponsor-owned, so there is no independent platform-grade T&D candidate. Vegetation managers (Asplundh, Davey, Lewis, Wright) score 3 because the work is thin-margin and re-bid. Dropped for having no verified website: East Coast Power (A&M Capital, 2025) and United Utility Services (Sandbrook/Blackstone, 2026); both would score platform-grade and sponsored, so restoring them makes platform-grade 4 and sponsored 5. J.W. Didado was dropped as a probable Quanta Services (NYSE: PWR) subsidiary, unverified.

Only 2 are independent, and both are unlikely sellers. METHOD (no web search; uses only the upstream lists plus limited, flagged background knowledge). Input: 85 entries. Output: 51 candidates. 4 entries were folded into others as duplicates and 30 were dropped.

MERGES: (1) Sparus Holdings, gas entry plus T&D entry (Allegiant, TruCheck). (2) Michels, gas, T&D and water entries, now one gas entry. (3) Hydromax USA (water) folded into Pro-Vac (gas). This last merge rests on the URL of Pro-Vac's release ('pro-vac-completes-acquisition-of-hydromax') and is unconfirmed. If that release refers to a different Hydromax, re-add Hydromax USA as IGP-owned since Dec 2020, fit 3-4. Possible further overlap: both PURIS and IPR are attributed to J.F. Lehman.

DROPPED, PUBLIC-COMPANY SUBSIDIARY (1): J.W. Didado Electric. Background recollection says it is a Quanta Services operating company; verify before re-adding. No other input entry was public or a subsidiary of a public company. Portfolio companies of funds run by listed sponsors (Blackstone, TPG, EQT) are treated as PE-backed, not as public subsidiaries. Southwire, Novinium's owner, is private.

DEFINITIONS:
- fit_score: how well the business model fits the thesis criteria (recurring maintenance, customer quality and tenure, specialized labor and equipment, avoiding low-bid/fixed-price work, safety). Size and availability are handled in red_flags and independent_available, not in the score. Re-scored from the inputs:
  - Artera 3 to 4 (size moved to red flags)
  - Asplundh 4 to 3 (vegetation-management economics, consistent with Davey)
  - Spiniello 4 to 3 (low-bid)
  - M.E. Simpson 4 to 3 (unknowns)
  - Power Services Group 4 to 3 (unverified ownership, possible fixed-price turnkey outages)
  - PURIS 3 to 2 (project and bid work)
  - Azuria 1 to 3 (scored on business model; still a non-target)
  - Divergent Alliance 2 to 1
  - Pro-Vac/Hydromax merged entry scored 3
- independent_available:
  - yes: family, founder or employee-owned, with no sponsor.
  - partial: PE-held for more than about 3 years and not visibly building (only a secondary buyout is possible), or PE-held with an unknown entry date.
  - no: sponsor or strategic entry within about 3 years, a sponsor actively making acquisitions, or owned by a strategic.
  - unknown: ownership not verified.
- platform_grade: fit of 4 or more, AND recurring_maintenance yes or partial, AND avoids_low_bid_fixed_price yes or partial. Unknown on either field does not qualify.
- addon_grade: classified as an add-on, fit of 2 or more, and not platform-grade.
- already_sponsored: a current PE or infrastructure-fund owner per the sources. Strategic owners are not counted, and neither is an unverified current owner.

KEY FINDINGS FOR THE REPORT:
(a) Platform-grade candidates: 14 across the four units. Only 3 are confirmed independent: Day & Zimmermann, Structural Integrity Associates and Carylon. D&Z and SIA are unlikely sellers. 3 more may be independent if ownership checks out: Heath Consultants, Pittsburg Tank & Tower and Maguire Iron. So the realistic pursue-now list from this research is about 1-4 names. The candidate universe needs primary-source deepening before claiming a pipeline, using the DCA, NETA, NASSCO and AWWA member directories and state PUC and utility contractor lists.
(b) Sponsor-backed platforms already in this space: 17 kept plus 9 dropped, 26 in all. Kept: Pike, Osmose, Artera, USIC, Sparus, Pro-Vac/Hydromax, GPT, Premium Utility Contractor, Shermco, RESA, Allied, EthosEnergy, USG, Visu-Sewer, HK Solutions, PURIS, Azuria. Dropped: East Coast Power, United Utility Services, Precision Pipeline Services, SI Solutions, XCEL NDT, RJ Underground, Delphi, IPR, Federal EC. These show the roll-up model works, and that there is heavy sponsor competition for add-ons. They also undercut the deck's '<10 meaningful scaled players' unless 'scaled' means national multi-billion players only. Public consolidators (Quanta, MasTec, MYR, Primoris, Centuri, Dycom and others) are excluded from this list by rule but belong in the competition analysis.
(c) T&D is the most picked-over unit: no independent platform-grade name. Water and power-gen NDE/testing have the most independent mid-size operators.
(d) Many fields are 'unknown' because of thin sourcing. Treat fit scores of 3 with mostly unknown criteria as 'not yet diligenced', not as 'weak'.

nodes.name: Itron

nodes.size_label: Revenue ~$2.4B (2024, approx.); US utility slice est. $1.0-1.7B

nodes.name: Utility pipe makers (JM Eagle, WL Plastics, Westlake Pipe & Fittings, Diamond Plastics, McWane, U.S. Pipe, American Cast Iron Pipe)
nodes.description: PE gas pipe, PVC and ductile-iron water and sewer pipe. Most moves through distributors; utilities often furnish the pipe their contractors install.

nodes.name: Gas fittings, valves and regulators (GF Central Plastics, Kerotest, Dresser Utility Solutions, Mueller gas products, Honeywell/Elster)
nodes.description: Electrofusion and mechanical fittings, service and curb valves, regulators and meter-set parts for gas mains and services. Bodies are mostly ductile iron, steel, brass or PE; stainless is a niche.

nodes.name: Power cable and conductor makers (Southwire, Prysmian incl. General Cable and Encore Wire, Okonite, Nexans)
nodes.description: Overhead conductor and URD/feeder cable for reconductoring, undergrounding and cable-replacement programs.

nodes.name: Poles and line hardware (Stella-Jones, Koppers, Valmont, Hubbell Utility Solutions, MacLean Power Systems, Preformed Line Products)
nodes.description: Wood and steel poles, crossarms, insulators and connectors. 130-160M wood poles are in service; maintained poles last 70-80+ years versus ~35-year book life.

nodes.name: Insurance and surety (Liberty Mutual, Travelers, Chubb, Zurich; brokers Marsh, Aon, WTW)
nodes.description: Auto, general liability, workers' comp and wildfire exposure for field contractors; a fast-rising cost (Davey took a $34.5M insurance charge in FY2025). Typically 2-4% of contractor revenue (assumption).

nodes.name: Field craft labor (IBEW outside line, LIUNA, UA, IUOE and open-shop crews)
nodes.description: Wages and benefits of lineworkers, gas crews, pipe layers and operators; 45-55% of contractor revenue. NAICS 237130 alone employs 292,604 people at an average $90,207 (CBP 2023 via aggregator). Crews and qualifications rarely transfer between gas, electric and water.

nodes.name: Badger Infrastructure Solutions
nodes.description: Largest hydrovac (non-destructive excavation) provider; builds its own trucks. Works for utilities directly and as a subcontractor to contractors. FY2025 revenue $831.7M, adj. EBITDA 23.8%, revenue per truck per month $41,672.

nodes.name: Restoration, paving and traffic-control subs (e.g., AWP Safety, Flagger Force, local paving firms)
nodes.description: Street restoration, paving and flagging after main and service replacement; a large share of urban replacement cost (assumption: 10-25%).

nodes.name: Core & Main
nodes.description: Largest US waterworks distributor: pipe, valves, hydrants, fittings and meters to municipalities and contractors.

nodes.name: Ferguson (Waterworks)
nodes.description: Waterworks is one of Ferguson's customer groups; supplies water and sewer contractors and utilities.

nodes.name: MRC Global
nodes.description: Pipe, valves and fittings distributor with a large gas-utility business (PE pipe, fittings, meters under MRO supply contracts). Merger with DNOW announced Jun 2025 (status not re-verified).

nodes.name: Wesco (Utility & Broadband Solutions)
nodes.description: Utility MRO materials (cable, connectors, line hardware, poles) and storm-stock programs for IOUs and co-ops. UBS segment $5.5B (2025) incl. broadband.

nodes.name: Quanta Services
nodes.description: The original 1990s utility-services roll-up and the category leader: electric T&D, underground utility (gas distribution, pipeline integrity) and renewables. Even at this scale adj. EBITDA is ~10.1%; scale bought labor depth, MSA share and backlog ($43.98B), not premium margins.
nodes.size_label: FY2025 revenue $28.48B; in-scope MRO flows est. $7.2-12.0B

nodes.name: MasTec
nodes.description: Diversified infrastructure contractor. Power Delivery $4,176M at 8.1% segment EBITDA; Pipeline $2,138M at 14.9% (down from 18.3%). Absorbed the IEA renewables roll-up in 2022 (~$1.1B EV).
nodes.size_label: FY2025 revenue $14.3B, adj. EBITDA 8.0%; in-scope est. $1.7-2.9B

nodes.name: Primoris Services
nodes.description: Utilities segment (power delivery, gas operations, communications) ~$2.69B at 11.5% gross margin; the Energy segment is EPC construction.
nodes.size_label: FY2025 revenue ~$7.7B, adj. EBITDA ~6.9%; in-scope est. $1.7-2.5B

nodes.name: MYR Group
nodes.description: T&D segment $2.00B at a 7.4% operating margin; gross margin swung 8.6% to 11.6% on project write-downs, showing fixed-price risk.

nodes.name: Michels Corporation
nodes.description: Family-owned diversified contractor (Brownsville WI): gas distribution, power lines and trenchless water rehab. ENR Top 400 #38 and #9 power contractor; revenue undisclosed. Water work folded into the regional water flows.

nodes.name: Centuri Holdings
nodes.description: Closest public analogue to the thesis: gas and electric utility MSA replacement work, spun out of Southwest Gas (separation completed 2025). Base gross margin only 8.0%; adj. EBITDA 8.3%; net leverage cut to 2.5x.

nodes.name: Artera Services (Miller Pipeline, Minnesota Limited, Feeney)
nodes.description: Gas-first MRO roll-up: bought CenterPoint's Miller Pipeline and Minnesota Limited for $850M (2020). Moody's cut to Caa1 (2022) and S&P to CCC+ negative (Dec 2025): the most direct warning for a leveraged gas MRO platform. Also does water rehab and pipeline integrity (integrity not shown).

nodes.name: Energy Services of America
nodes.description: Small public gas and water distribution contractor in Appalachia: a scale reference for a FAM platform. Adj. EBITDA fell to 4.2% in FY2025.

nodes.name: Pike Corporation
nodes.description: T&D maintenance, storm restoration and engineering, ~12,000 employees, 400+ customers. TPG Rise Climate and La Caisse bought a majority from Lindsay Goldberg in Dec 2025 at a reported >$5B (unconfirmed). Revenue was ~$1.7B in 2020.

nodes.name: Asplundh Tree Expert
nodes.description: Largest utility vegetation-management and line-clearance firm; also line construction. Revenue ~$6.3B per Forbes (weak; other sources $4.5-4.7B), incl. non-US and non-utility work.

nodes.name: Davey Tree Expert
nodes.description: Employee-owned; utility vegetation management is its largest segment. FY2025 operating margin ~3.7% (5.5% ex a $34.5M insurance charge): recurring revenue, thin margins.

nodes.name: Osmose Utilities Services
nodes.description: Pole inspection, treatment and restoration (incl. co-ops); the 10-year inspect-and-treat cycle is what stretches pole life to 70-80+ years. Second sponsor (EQT, 2019).

nodes.name: USIC
nodes.description: Largest North American 811 locating and damage-prevention firm; bought Heath Consultants' gas-locating unit in 2025. The one proven cross-utility service, but a single service line. Only gas-utility locating is drawn; electric, water and telecom locates excluded.
nodes.size_label: Revenue not disclosed; gas locating est. $0.4-0.8B

nodes.name: Shermco Industries
nodes.description: NETA-accredited electrical testing roll-up: ~40 service centers, 600+ NETA technicians, built by buying regional NETA firms. Sold to Blackstone for ~$1.6B (Oct 2025); growth leaned on data centers and C&I.
nodes.size_label: Revenue not disclosed; est. $0.3-0.55B (from deal value, assumption)

nodes.name: Mistras Group
nodes.description: NDE and inspection consolidator; mostly oil and gas, with growing power generation. Stable but not growing; 12.6% adj. EBITDA.

nodes.name: Day & Zimmermann
nodes.description: ENR's #1 power O&M contractor for six straight years: nuclear and fossil outage maintenance and modifications. Outage work needs NRC Appendix B quality programs, a high entry barrier.

nodes.name: Team Inc
nodes.description: Inspection, heat treating and mechanical services, mostly refining and petrochemical; power is a minority. Net loss in FY2025 after a 2025 refinancing.

nodes.name: OEM field services (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi Power, Westinghouse, Framatome, Vestas)
nodes.description: Long-term service agreements and outage services by equipment makers. They capture the largest share of plant maintenance and sit outside the addressable pool for an independent roll-up.

nodes.name: Independent plant maintenance contractors (EnergySolutions incl. ex-Williams, BrandSafway, Babcock & Wilcox services, regional outage firms)
nodes.description: Non-OEM outage, boiler, balance-of-plant and renewable O&M work. Williams Industrial Services (nuclear and fossil maintenance plus water) went through Chapter 11 in 2023 and sold to EnergySolutions for $60M.

nodes.name: Azuria Water Solutions (Insituform) + Inframark
nodes.description: Ex-Aegion, taken private by New Mountain in 2021 ($963M announced) and refocused on water; CIPP sewer and water rehab plus Inframark contract O&M. Combination announced Jul 2025 at ~$2.5B combined revenue.
nodes.size_label: ~$2.5B combined revenue; US municipal flows est. $1.3-1.9B

nodes.name: Vortex Companies
nodes.description: Trenchless water and sewer rehab roll-up (~12 acquisitions); bought Tri-State Utilities and Pipe Vision from National Underground Group.

nodes.name: National Underground Group
nodes.description: ORIX-backed sewer inspection, cleaning and trenchless rehab platform.

nodes.name: USG Water Solutions (Utility Service Co)
nodes.description: Long-term water-tank maintenance contracts with municipalities; sold to Suez/United Water for $220M in 2008 (current owner not re-verified; likely Veolia after its Suez merger).

nodes.name: Regional gas and pipeline contractors (long tail)
nodes.description: Thousands of small and mid-size gas main, service and integrity contractors inside NAICS 237120/237110; part of ~18,877 utility-system construction firms (2017 Economic Census via NUCA). The pool FAM would buy from.

nodes.name: Regional line, vegetation and NETA testing firms (long tail)
nodes.description: Regional line contractors, tree crews and NETA-accredited testing firms (NAICS 237130: 7,112 establishments; includes telecom). Shermco's add-on pool.

nodes.name: Regional water and sewer contractors (long tail)
nodes.description: Main replacement, lead service-line, CIPP and valve/hydrant crews (NAICS 237110: ~10,600 firms). Most fragmented unit; buyers are municipal.

nodes.name: Atmos Energy
nodes.description: Largest gas-only US distributor (8 states). Spends most of its capex (~$3.6B in FY2025, approx.; not re-verified) on safety and reliability replacement, recovered through rate riders.

nodes.name: Southwest Gas
nodes.description: AZ, NV and CA gas utility and Centuri's former parent; still a major Centuri customer.

nodes.name: CenterPoint Energy (gas utilities)
nodes.description: Sold Miller Pipeline and Minnesota Limited (its in-house contractors) to PowerTeam/Artera in 2020 for $850M; continued work with them is likely but not verified.

nodes.name: Other gas LDCs (NiSource, Southern Company Gas, Spire, ONE Gas, National Grid, Con Edison, PSEG and others)
nodes.description: 1,367,851 miles of main (2023). Cast and wrought iron is ~1% of mains but 8% of main incidents; 16,337 miles left (2023), concentrated in NJ, NY, MA, PA and MI. Gas utilities invest ~$33-37B a year in safety.

nodes.name: PG&E
nodes.description: Electric and gas IOU. Its 1921 Caribou-Palermo line (~97 years old) started the 2018 Camp Fire; now spends heavily on vegetation management, undergrounding and hardening.

nodes.name: Duke Energy
nodes.description: Large Southeast IOU; historically Pike's largest customer (per past Pike filings; not re-verified).

nodes.name: Other electric IOUs (AEP, Southern, Dominion, Xcel, Exelon, FirstEnergy, Entergy and others)
nodes.description: EEI members plan ~$208B of capex in 2025 and >$1.1T over 2025-29; distribution capex $50.9B (2023), transmission $32.6B (2024). Only replacement, hardening and outsourced O&M is in scope.

nodes.name: Public power and co-ops (~2,000 municipal utilities, ~900 co-ops, TVA)
nodes.description: Serve ~28% of US retail kWh; buy line maintenance, vegetation and pole inspection, often from regional firms.

nodes.name: Constellation Energy
nodes.description: Largest US nuclear fleet; restarting Crane (ex-TMI-1, target 2027) under a Microsoft PPA and signed a Clinton PPA with Meta (per company announcements; not re-verified). Life extension locks in decades of refueling outages.

nodes.name: Other nuclear operators (Duke, Southern Nuclear, TVA, Vistra, Dominion, PSEG, Entergy, NextEra, Talen, Holtec)
nodes.description: NRC renewed 18 licenses (~17 GW) in 15 months; 80-year licenses now routine (Turkey Point, Surry, Browns Ferry, St. Lucie, Hatch). Regulated units' revenue sits in the tariff edges, so only merchant output is drawn to markets.

nodes.name: Gas and coal plant owners (IOUs and IPPs: Vistra, NRG and others)
nodes.description: Gas turbines run harder as load grows; the coal fleet averages 45 years and retires at ~50, so coal is a shrinking maintenance market.

nodes.name: Wind, solar and storage owners (NextEra Energy Resources, AES, Invenergy, Brookfield and others)
nodes.description: 53 GW added in 2025 and 86 GW planned for 2026; O&M pool est. $7-10B, largely captured by OEM service agreements and owners' in-house teams.

nodes.name: American Water Works
nodes.description: Largest US investor-owned water and wastewater utility; most capex goes to main replacement, recovered through PUC rates.

nodes.name: Municipal water and wastewater utilities (~50,000 community water systems, ~16,000 treatment works)
nodes.description: 33% of mains are >50 years old; 11.1 breaks per 100 miles a year; replacement pace implies a ~125-year cycle. EPA's 20-year need is $625B ($420.8B distribution); ~4.0M lead service lines (2025 update). Most O&M is in-house.

nodes.name: Gas transmission pipeline operators (Kinder Morgan, Williams, Energy Transfer, TC Energy)
nodes.description: Integrity digs, in-line inspection follow-up and maintenance; adjacent to, not inside, the thesis TAM.
nodes.size_label: Integrity and maintenance services in est. $1.4-3.0B

nodes.name: Data-center and C&I electrical owners
nodes.description: Owners of behind-the-meter substations and switchgear that buy NETA acceptance and maintenance testing; Shermco's fastest-growing customers. Outside the thesis TAM.

nodes.name: PUC-regulated electric tariffs (IOU rate base)
nodes.description: Capitalized replacement earns a regulated return in rate base; O&M does not. That is why replacement work under MSAs is the sturdier pool.

nodes.name: PUC-regulated gas tariffs (incl. infrastructure-replacement riders)
nodes.description: Replacement programs are recovered through riders and surcharges outside full rate cases. The federal leak-detection rule is not in force (withdrawn Jan 2025; new proposal sent to DOT Apr 2026).

nodes.name: Public power and co-op rates (local boards)
nodes.description: Rates set by city councils, utility boards and co-op members.

nodes.name: Water and sewer rates and municipal revenue bonds
nodes.description: Public water and wastewater spending was $113B in 2017 ($31B capital, $82B O&M); capital is largely bond-financed and repaid from rates.

nodes.name: Federal water programs (Clean Water and Drinking Water SRFs, IIJA supplemental, WIFIA)
nodes.description: FY2026 is the last year of IIJA supplemental SRF money ($2,603M each fund). Regular FY2026 funding is flat but earmarks leave net grants of ~$746M (CWSRF) and ~$411M (DWSRF): a federal cliff in FY2027.
nodes.size_label: FY2026 financing est. $10-18B incl. state match and revolving loans

nodes.name: Wholesale power markets and PPAs (ISO/RTO, bilateral)
nodes.description: Merchant generators sell energy and capacity here; PJM wholesale prices +~41% in 2026 (EIA STEO). Utilities' purchases for default service are embedded in the tariff edges, so this node is not additive with them.

nodes.name: Large-load tariffs and customer contributions (data centers)
nodes.description: Data-center electricity bills and contributions in aid of construction for interconnections; growth is concentrated in ERCOT and PJM and pays mostly for new construction, not maintenance.

nodes.name: Households (residential ratepayers)
nodes.description: Residential electricity revenue was $244.4B in 2024; residential use per customer fell 2.3% from 2009 to 2019 on efficiency. US population growth slowed to 0.5% in 2025, so households are not the growth driver.
nodes.size_label: Electricity $244.4B (2024) plus gas and water bills

nodes.name: Businesses and industry (commercial and industrial ratepayers)
nodes.description: Commercial ($185.0B) and industrial ($84.1B) electricity revenue in 2024, plus gas and water bills. Commercial sales lead 2026 growth at +3.8% (incl. data centers).
nodes.size_label: Electricity $269B (2024) plus gas and water bills

nodes.name: Data centers and hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta)
nodes.description: Data centers used 176 TWh in 2023 (4.4% of US use), heading to 325-580 TWh by 2028 (LBNL). Nuclear PPAs include Constellation-Microsoft (Crane), Constellation-Meta (Clinton) and Talen-Amazon (Susquehanna) (per company announcements; not re-verified).

nodes.name: Federal and state taxpayers
nodes.description: Fund SRF capitalization grants (federal) and the 20% state match; only ~4% of public water spending was federal in 2017.

network.notes:
The network has 85 nodes (5 Fulton) and 146 edges: 138 flows and 8 Fulton opportunities. Every edge runs left to right. No web search was used; the network is built from the research input and general knowledge. The build script and its checks are at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-claude-shit/1e3ac4f9-9e01-5ae6-b622-1de6e18f143d/scratchpad/vc/build_vc.py, and its output is vc.json in the same folder.

LAYOUT CHOICE
- Funding sits on the right, not in S3. C2 "Funding channels" holds the PUC electric and gas tariffs, public-power rates, water/sewer rates and municipal bonds, federal SRF/IIJA/WIFIA money, wholesale markets and large-load contracts. C3 "Ultimate payers" holds households, businesses, hyperscalers and taxpayers.
- This keeps money flowing between adjacent columns and avoids counting ratepayer money twice. S3 instead holds raw inputs, truck chassis and the craft-training pipeline.
- The body.html subtitle for #value-chain says "who funds the work" comes first. It should be reworded to match this layout.
- The shared SVG code still hard-codes "Builders" over column B and a transformer aria-label. Both should be changed to "Service providers".

SANITY CHECKS AGAINST THE TAM RESEARCH
Service flows from B (plus Badger direct) to C1, by business unit:

| Unit | Flows in map | TAM in research |
|---|---|---|
| Gas | $11.1-19.6B | $12-20B |
| T&D | $20.1-34.0B | $20-35B |
| Independent power-gen maintenance | $3.9-6.8B | $4-8B |
| Water | $7.7-15.6B | $8-18B |
| Four-unit total | $42.8-76.0B | $44-81B |

- OEM long-term service work is drawn but sits outside the TAM: $2.3-4.6B for nuclear and fossil plants, and $1.5-3B for wind.
- Context flows also outside the TAM: pipeline integrity $1.1-2.4B, data-center and C&I testing $0.8-1.6B, and independent renewables O&M $0.3-0.8B.
- The long-tail aggregates (regional gas, line and water) are each unit's TAM minus the named firms, so they do not overlap them.
- Named-firm flows were checked against disclosed revenue or segments:
  - Quanta $7.2-12.0B in-scope out of $28.48B revenue.
  - Centuri $2.05-2.8B out of $2.98B.
  - Artera $1.65-2.5B out of more than $2.6B.
  - MasTec, Primoris and MYR use their segment figures.
- Funding channel balances (inflow vs outflow):

| Channel | In | Out |
|---|---|---|
| Electric tariffs | $264.5-319.5B | $260-320B |
| Gas tariffs | $105-139B | $110-140B |
| Water rates | $95-125B | $95-125B |

- The C3 totals roughly match EIA's 2024 retail electricity revenue: $244.4B residential and $269B commercial plus industrial.

DOUBLE-COUNTING CAVEATS
- Ten edges skip from S2 straight to C1: meters, cable, poles, utility fleets and sewer trucks. These are materials the utility buys itself, not services, and are outside the services TAM. Paths that go through distributors are separate amounts from direct maker-to-utility sales.
- Field-labor edges are payroll that sits inside contractor revenue. They are an input, not additional spending.
- Wholesale inflows ($77-136B) exceed outflows ($60-112B). Utilities' default-service power purchases are already embedded in the tariff edges, and revenue from regulated plants sits in the IOU and public-power tariffs.

WEAK OR UNVERIFIED ITEMS
- Undisclosed revenue, inferred from deal value, headcount or segment mix: Asplundh (Forbes figure, weak), Pike, USIC, Osmose, Shermco, Vortex, National Underground Group, USG and Michels.

  - Quanta's ownership of Northwest Lineman College.
