  - The nuclear PPAs: Crane/Microsoft, Clinton/Meta and Susquehanna/Amazon.
  - Atmos and American Water capex.
  - Utility revenues on the C1-to-C2 edges.
  - Current owner of USG Water Solutions.

FULTON
- The eight Fulton edges are addressable markets, not current sales.
- Cast-iron main scrap is small ($10-45M) because most retired cast iron is abandoned in place or used as a casing for inserted plastic pipe. Ferrous scrap is also outside Imperial's non-ferrous core.
- The best metals angles:
  - Cable copper and aluminum: $150-500M. This overlaps the reconductoring scrap in the transformer map's f2 edge.
  - Lead service-line pipe and brass meters: $30-80M. This depends on the pending D.C. Circuit ruling on LCRI.
- SFE's stainless castings fit niche valve bodies ($3-30M) and outage replacement parts ($20-90M; nuclear parts need Appendix B qualification) better than commodity valves.
- Panther ($25-100M) and AFCO ($15-100M, via Altec truck bodies) have chain-wide pools, but realistic share is small.
- Transend's pipe freight ($80-270M) is standard flatbed work and needs no heavy-haul capability.
- The three Imperial edges run from S3 straight to C1, as Fulton edges did in the transformer map.

terms.definition: A gas utility that owns the low-pressure mains and service lines that deliver natural gas to homes and businesses in its franchise area, such as Atmos Energy or Southern California Gas. LDCs are the main buyers of leak survey, locating and gas pipe replacement work.

A utility owned by shareholders and regulated by a state utility commission, such as Duke Energy or American Water Works. IOUs serve about 70% of US electricity customers and earn a regulated return on the capital they invest, which rewards replacing old pipe and wire.

A utility owned by a city or other local government, such as the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. About 2,000 US electric utilities (known as public power) are publicly owned, as are the systems serving most Americans' drinking water; they usually buy services through public, low-bid procurement.

A not-for-profit utility owned by its members, mostly in rural areas. About 900 US electric co-ops serve roughly 13% of electricity customers but own about 42% of distribution line miles, so they are large buyers of line work and right-of-way clearing.

A company that owns power plants and sells electricity into wholesale markets or under contract rather than to retail customers, such as Vistra or Constellation. IPPs buy outage, inspection and testing services for their plants.

EPA's term for a public water system that serves the same residents year-round, such as a town or city. There are roughly 50,000 in the US, but a few thousand large systems serve most of the population.

The Clean Water Act term for a municipal wastewater system, including its sewer pipes and treatment plant. There are about 16,000 in the US, and their sewer rehabilitation needs drive CIPP and sewer inspection work.

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which regulates interstate electricity transmission, wholesale power markets and interstate gas pipelines. It also collects the FERC Form 1 financial reports used to estimate utility maintenance spending.

The North American Electric Reliability Corporation, which writes and enforces mandatory reliability standards for the high-voltage grid under FERC oversight. Its standards require periodic testing of protection systems, vegetation clearing along transmission lines and cybersecurity controls.

The US Environmental Protection Agency, which sets national drinking-water standards such as the lead and PFAS rules, regulates sewage discharges, and runs the State Revolving Funds and the water and wastewater needs surveys.
The Department of Energy's independent statistics agency. It publishes electricity demand, generation, power plant and utility data through survey forms such as EIA-860 and EIA-861.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Labor Department agency that publishes employment, wage, workplace injury and price data, including the OEWS and QCEW programs.

The Commerce Department agency that counts businesses as well as people. Its County Business Patterns, Statistics of US Businesses and Economic Census report company and location counts by industry code, the basis for checking how fragmented a market is.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission, which licenses and inspects US nuclear plants. License renewals now let many reactors run for 60 to 80 years, which sustains demand for refueling-outage inspection and maintenance work.
The American Gas Association, the trade group for US gas utilities. It publishes industry statistics, including utility spending on safety and pipe replacement.

The American Water Works Association, the main professional body for drinking-water utilities. It publishes technical standards and widely cited estimates of pipe replacement needs, such as its "Buried No Longer" report.

A grade card for US infrastructure that the American Society of Civil Engineers publishes about every four years, most recently in 2025. It comes from an engineering advocacy group, so its grades and funding-gap figures are estimates rather than official data.

The trade association for sewer and pipeline rehabilitation contractors. Its PACP standard is the common way of coding sewer pipe condition from CCTV video (MACP covers manholes and LACP laterals), and its certifications are often required in sewer inspection bids.

The InterNational Electrical Testing Association, which publishes the standards for acceptance testing of new electrical equipment (ATS) and maintenance testing of equipment in service (MTS). It also accredits testing companies and certifies their technicians, who form the core of the electrical testing segment.

aliases: Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration
terms.definition: The Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, the Department of Transportation agency that sets federal safety rules for gas and hazardous-liquid pipelines (49 CFR Parts 192 and 195). State utility commissions enforce most of its rules on gas distribution utilities.

The state agency, called a public utility or public service commission depending on the state, that sets the rates investor-owned utilities may charge and approves their spending plans. Its decisions largely determine how much utilities spend on replacement and maintenance.

The formal proceeding in which a utility asks its state commission to change its prices based on its costs and invested capital. A rate case typically takes about a year, and utilities plan maintenance and replacement budgets around the outcome.

The value of a regulated utility's invested capital, net of depreciation, on which regulators let it earn a return. Replacing pipe or poles adds to rate base while routine maintenance is an expense, so utilities have a financial incentive to replace rather than repair.
The profit rate on shareholder capital that a state commission lets a utility earn on its rate base, recently around 9.5% to 10% for US electric and gas utilities.

A surcharge on customer bills, approved by a state commission, that lets a utility recover the cost of pipe or wire replacement between rate cases. Most states have one for gas pipe replacement; Pennsylvania's DSIC (Distribution System Improvement Charge) is a common water and gas example.

PHMSA's Distribution Integrity Management Program rule (49 CFR Part 192, Subpart P), in force since 2011, which requires every gas distribution utility to identify the threats to its pipes, rank the risks and act to reduce them. It underpins the leak survey and pipe replacement programs that drive gas services demand.

PHMSA's integrity management rule for gas transmission pipelines (49 CFR Part 192, Subpart O), which requires operators to assess pipe in populated "high consequence areas" by in-line inspection, pressure testing or direct assessment and to repair what they find. It drives inspection, NDE and dig-and-repair work.

The Protecting our Infrastructure of Pipelines and Enhancing Safety Act of 2020, which reauthorized PHMSA. It requires gas operators to run leak detection and repair programs and to update maintenance plans to minimize methane releases, and led to PHMSA's 2023 proposed leak detection and repair rule.

EPA's October 2024 update to the Lead and Copper Rule, which requires most water systems to replace all lead and galvanized-requiring-replacement service lines within ten years of its November 2027 compliance date. It builds on the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR), which required every system to inventory its service lines; its deadlines could still change through litigation or EPA review.

A list, required from every community water system by October 2024, classifying each service line as lead, galvanized requiring replacement, non-lead or unknown material. Many states publish them, giving a count of lines needing replacement.

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, long-lasting industrial chemicals ("forever chemicals") found in many water supplies. EPA set the first national drinking-water limits in 2024, including 4 parts per trillion for PFOA and PFOS; in 2025 it said it would keep those two limits but move compliance from 2029 to 2031 and reconsider the others. Compliance mostly means new treatment plants rather than pipe work.
The 1974 federal law under which EPA sets enforceable standards for public drinking water, including the lead and PFAS rules.
The 1972 federal law that regulates discharges into US waters. Sewer overflows violate it, which is why many cities operate under consent decrees requiring sewer rehabilitation.

A court-approved settlement, often between EPA and a city, that commits the city to fix sewer overflows on a fixed schedule, typically over 10 to 25 years at a cost of hundreds of millions to billions of dollars. It makes sewer rehabilitation spending legally mandatory rather than discretionary.

The Clean Water and Drinking Water State Revolving Funds, through which EPA gives grants to states that then make low-interest loans, and sometimes grants, to water and sewer systems for capital projects. The IIJA added about $43 billion to them over five years, including $15 billion for lead service line replacement.

The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of November 2021, also called the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, which authorized about $1.2 trillion including roughly $550 billion of new federal spending over fiscal 2022 to 2026. It funded water systems (about $55 billion), grid resilience and gas pipe replacement grants, and its five-year funding ends with fiscal 2026 unless renewed.

aliases: Natural Gas Distribution Infrastructure Safety and Modernization
terms.definition: The Natural Gas Distribution Infrastructure Safety and Modernization grant program, created by the IIJA with $1 billion over five years for municipal and community-owned gas utilities to replace leak-prone pipe. PHMSA administers it.

An IIJA provision requiring iron, steel, manufactured products and construction materials used in federally funded infrastructure projects, including SRF-funded water work, to be made in the US unless a waiver is granted.

The 2022 climate and tax law that expanded tax credits for solar, wind, storage, nuclear and other clean energy. The July 2025 tax law cut back its wind and solar credits while largely keeping those for nuclear, storage and geothermal.

The July 2025 federal tax and spending law. Among other things it ends federal tax credits for wind and solar projects that do not start construction by July 2026 or enter service by the end of 2027, which may pull solar additions forward and then slow them.

NERC's Critical Infrastructure Protection standards, mandatory cybersecurity and physical-security rules for the systems and sites that run the high-voltage grid. CIP-014, for example, requires physical protection of the most critical substations.

The NERC standard requiring owners of the high-voltage grid to test and maintain protective relays, station batteries and related equipment within set maximum intervals. It creates recurring, non-discretionary demand for relay testing.

A utility plan, required in California and a growing number of other western states, for reducing the risk that power lines start wildfires through vegetation clearing, line inspection, covered conductor and undergrounding. These plans have sharply increased vegetation management spending in the West.

A multi-year framework contract under which a utility issues a stream of work orders to a contractor at pre-agreed prices without rebidding each job. MSAs typically run three to five years and make revenue recurring, though they rarely guarantee volume. In Census data, MSA instead means metropolitan statistical area.

A contract that pays a fixed price per unit of work, such as per foot of pipe installed, per leak repaired or per pole replaced, so revenue depends on volume. It is the most common pricing in utility MSAs and rewards contractors whose crews are productive.

A contract that pays hourly rates for labor and equipment plus the cost of materials, usually with a markup. It is common for emergency and storm work, where the scope is unknown in advance, and carries little cost-overrun risk for the contractor.
A contract that reimburses the contractor's actual costs plus a fixed fee or percentage. It moves cost risk to the customer but usually caps the contractor's margin.
A contract that pays one agreed price for a defined scope of work. The contractor keeps any savings but absorbs cost overruns, so margins are more volatile than under unit-price or T&M work.

Public purchasing in which the contract goes to the qualified bidder offering the lowest price. Cities and other public owners must usually buy this way, which limits pricing power compared with negotiated MSAs from investor-owned utilities.

A screening step before a contractor may bid on or work for a utility, typically checking safety record (TRIR, EMR), insurance, bonding capacity, Operator Qualification and finances. Getting on a utility's approved list can take months, which protects incumbents and makes acquired customer relationships valuable.

A guarantee from an insurance company that a contractor will finish the job (performance bond) and pay its suppliers and subcontractors (payment bond). Public projects usually require bonds, and a contractor's bonding capacity, which the surety sets from its balance sheet, caps how much public work it can take on.

A share of each payment, typically 5% to 10%, that the customer holds back until a project is complete. It ties up contractor cash and is common on public project work but less so on utility MSA work.
Spending to keep existing assets working, as opposed to building new ones. In this report it means recurring inspection, testing, repair and replacement work on utility pipes, wires and plants.

A utility's day-to-day running and upkeep costs, which it recovers in rates without earning a return. Leak survey, locating and vegetation management are mostly O&M, while pipe and pole replacement is usually capital spending.

Spending on long-lived assets, which a utility adds to its rate base and recovers over decades with a return. Investor-owned utility capex is at record levels, and replacing aging pipe and wire is a large share of it.

Periodic checking of gas pipes for leaks, by technicians walking the lines with gas detectors or by vehicles carrying sensitive methane analyzers ("advanced leak detection"). Federal rules require surveys at least every five years in most areas and every year in business districts, and many utilities survey more often.

The industry practice of classifying gas leaks by danger: Grade 1 is hazardous and repaired immediately, Grade 2 is not hazardous now but scheduled for repair, and Grade 3 is non-hazardous and monitored. Utilities report hazardous leaks repaired each year to PHMSA, one public measure of pipe condition.

terms.term: Cast iron and bare steel pipe
terms.definition: Older gas main materials prone to cracking and corrosion: cast iron, laid mostly in the first half of the 20th century, and steel without cathodic protection, which became mandatory in 1971. PHMSA annual reports track the miles of each material that remain, by utility and state, and regulators push utilities to replace them.

Plastic pipe that is now the standard material for new and replacement gas distribution lines and is widely used for water. It does not corrode, and its joints are fused with heat by fusion machines run by qualified workers.

The larger pipe running under streets that carries gas or water through a neighborhood, from which service lines branch to each building. The US has about 1.3 million miles of gas distribution main and roughly 2.2 million miles of water pipe; a main break is a rupture of a water main.
The small pipe connecting a gas or water main under the street to an individual building. Service lines are where most remaining lead pipe sits in water systems and where many gas leaks occur.

Inspection of a pipeline from the inside by a sensor-laden device (a "smart pig") that travels with the gas or oil flow and records corrosion, dents and cracks. It is the main assessment method for transmission pipelines; most distribution pipe is too small and branched for it.

A test in which a pipeline section is filled with water and pressurized above its operating pressure to prove it will not fail. PHMSA's 2019 gas transmission rule requires many older pipelines without adequate records to be pressure-tested or otherwise reverified.
An excavation to expose a pipeline section flagged by inspection so crews can examine it, often with NDE, and repair or replace it. Integrity digs combine excavation, NDE and pipeline welding skills.

A way of preventing corrosion on buried steel pipe by applying a small electric current, from rectifiers or sacrificial metal anodes, so the pipe does not lose metal. Federal rules require it on steel gas pipelines along with periodic surveys to confirm it works, which is recurring specialist work.

Methods for inspecting welds, pipe walls and equipment without damaging them, such as ultrasonic, radiographic (X-ray), magnetic-particle and eddy-current testing. Technicians are certified by method and level, so NDE crews are specialized and not easily swapped with general construction crews.

Methods for installing, renewing or replacing underground pipe without digging a continuous trench, including HDD, CIPP, sliplining and pipe bursting. They reduce street disruption and are now standard for urban sewer and water work.

A trenchless repair in which a resin-soaked fabric tube is inserted into a damaged pipe and hardened with hot water, steam or ultraviolet light, forming a new pipe inside the old one. It is the dominant method for rehabilitating sewer mains and a specialized, equipment-heavy niche.

A trenchless repair that pushes or pulls a slightly smaller new pipe, usually plastic, inside an existing pipe and fills the gap with grout. It is simple and inexpensive but reduces the pipe's capacity.

A trenchless replacement method that pulls a bursting head through an old pipe, breaking it outward while drawing a new pipe of the same or larger size into its place. It is widely used for lead service line and water main replacement.

Inspection of sewer pipes with a remote-controlled camera crawler driven through the line, with defects coded, typically to NASSCO's PACP standard. Many cities inspect a set share of their sewers each year, and the findings drive rehabilitation work such as CIPP.

Rainwater and groundwater that enter sewer pipes through cracks, bad joints and improper connections. It overloads treatment plants and causes overflows, and reducing it is a main goal of sewer rehabilitation.

A discharge of untreated sewage, either from older combined sewers that carry stormwater and sewage in one pipe (CSO, in roughly 700 US communities) or from separate sanitary sewers that leak or back up (SSO). Both violate the Clean Water Act and are the usual target of EPA consent decrees.

Water a utility treats but never bills, mostly lost through leaks and main breaks, plus meter errors and theft. Many US systems lose 10% to 30% of their treated water, which supports leak detection and meter replacement work.
Finding leaks in buried water pipes by listening for leak noise with ground microphones, correlators or permanently installed sensors. It is a lower-cost way to cut water loss than replacing pipe.

Removing the lead pipes that connect water mains to homes and replacing them with copper or plastic, usually including the portion on private property. EPA estimated about 9.2 million lead service lines nationwide, and costs range from several thousand to tens of thousands of dollars per line depending on the city.

Digging with pressurized water to loosen soil, which a truck-mounted vacuum then sucks into a debris tank. It exposes buried pipes and cables without damaging them and is used across gas, water and electric work; a hydrovac truck typically costs several hundred thousand dollars.

Any excavation that removes soil by vacuum, after loosening it with water (hydro-excavation) or compressed air. It is the standard "soft dig" method for potholing, which exposes existing utilities to confirm their exact location before drilling or digging.

A truck that combines a high-pressure water jet to scour sewer pipes with a vacuum to remove the debris. It is the basic tool of sewer cleaning and is usually paired with CCTV inspection, but it is specific to sewer work.

Marking the location of buried pipes and cables with paint and flags before anyone digs, after a call to the national 811 "call before you dig" number. Utilities often outsource it to specialist contractors that handle millions of tickets a year, and locating errors lead to excavation damage, a leading cause of gas distribution incidents.

The two parts of the grid after the power plant: high-voltage transmission lines that move bulk power long distances, and lower-voltage distribution lines that deliver it to homes and businesses. Distribution has far more line miles and assets and accounts for most utility line maintenance.

A fenced site where transformers change voltage between transmission and distribution levels and circuit breakers and relays protect the lines. Substations are where most electrical testing work happens.
One thousand volts. US transmission lines typically run at 115 to 765 kV and distribution lines at roughly 4 to 35 kV.

A device that senses abnormal conditions on the grid, such as a short circuit, and signals circuit breakers to open, isolating the problem within a fraction of a second. Older electromechanical relays are being replaced by digital ones, which must be set, commissioned and periodically tested.

Checking that protective relays detect faults and trip breakers correctly, using portable test sets that inject simulated currents and voltages. NERC standard PRC-005 and utility maintenance programs require it on a recurring schedule; it is skilled technician work, often by NETA-certified staff.

Laboratory testing of the oil inside a transformer for gases that form when its insulation overheats or arcs, giving early warning of failure. Utilities sample large transformers periodically, making it a recurring service tied to transformer maintenance.

Inspection, repair and overhaul work done while a power plant is deliberately shut down, such as a nuclear plant's refueling outage every 18 to 24 months or a gas turbine's major inspection. The work comes in intense seasonal bursts, mostly spring and fall when power demand is low, and needs large, skilled temporary crews.

Trimming and removing trees and brush near power lines and keeping rights-of-way clear, usually on multi-year cycles. It is one of utilities' largest O&M costs, is mandatory for major transmission lines under NERC rules, and has grown sharply with wildfire plans; Asplundh is the largest provider.

Emergency repair of power lines after hurricanes, ice storms and other severe weather, often by contractor crews traveling from other regions under mutual assistance arrangements. It is billed at premium time-and-materials rates, profitable but highly variable from year to year.

Periodic testing of wooden utility poles for rot and damage, by sounding, boring and applying preservative, typically on cycles of about 8 to 12 years, with failed poles scheduled for replacement. The US has well over 100 million utility poles, most of them wood.
Moving overhead power lines into buried cable. It cuts wildfire and storm risk but costs several times more per mile than overhead line, so utilities target it to the highest-risk areas.

Networked "smart" meters that report usage to the utility automatically, plus the communications and data systems behind them; AMR is an older, one-way version. Roughly three-quarters of US electricity meters are now smart meters per EIA, while many gas and water utilities are still rolling them out, creating meter installation work.

Standard grid reliability measures: SAIDI is the average total minutes of outage per customer per year and SAIFI the average number of outages per customer. EIA reports both by utility, with and without "major event days" such as big storms, giving a public read on whether grid condition is improving or worsening.

Growth in electricity use or peak demand on the grid. US demand was roughly flat from about 2007 to 2021 as efficiency gains offset new uses, and is now rising again with data centers, factories and electrification.

A nuclear reactor of up to about 300 megawatts designed to be built in factory modules. None operates commercially in the US yet, and the first are expected around 2030 or later, so they matter little for near-term maintenance demand.

Solar or battery projects of about 1 megawatt or more that sell power to the grid, as opposed to rooftop systems. They need far less maintenance labor per megawatt than conventional plants, but each one adds substation and line assets that do need upkeep.

The number of years an asset is expected to last in normal service, such as roughly 40 to 50 years for transformers and wood poles and 50 to 100 years or more for many pipes. Assets often run past it with maintenance, so age alone overstates replacement need; each utility's depreciation study filed with regulators gives its own estimates.

The stock of assets that owners or regulators judge are due for replacement but have not yet been replaced, measured in miles of pipe, numbers of poles or dollars. It is different from a contractor's backlog of signed work.

The core vehicles of power-line work: a bucket truck lifts a lineworker up to the wires, and a digger derrick bores holes and sets poles. They are specific to electric line and tree work and are not used by gas or water crews.

Industry slang for general construction equipment such as excavators, backhoes, loaders and skid steers. It is the most interchangeable equipment across gas, water and electric underground work and is widely available to rent.

A trenchless method that drills a steerable bore underground and pulls new pipe or cable conduit through it, avoiding open trenches under roads, rivers and yards. Small HDD rigs are used for gas, water, electric and fiber work alike, making it one of the more transferable capabilities.

The share of available hours that equipment or workers are actually billed to customers. Higher utilization spreads fixed fleet and overhead costs over more revenue, and moving idle crews or trucks between business units is a common roll-up synergy claim.

PHMSA's rule (49 CFR Part 192, Subpart N, and Part 195, Subpart G) that anyone performing "covered tasks" on a pipeline, such as joining pipe, locating lines or checking cathodic protection, must be evaluated and qualified for each task. Qualifications are task-specific, which limits how freely crews can move between gas, water and electric work.

OSHA-recordable injuries and illnesses per 200,000 hours worked, roughly 100 full-time workers for a year. Utilities screen contractors on it, along with the DART rate (cases with days away, restricted work or job transfer) and lost-time rate, and BLS publishes industry averages for comparison.

A workers' compensation insurance factor that compares a company's past injury claims with the average for its industry: 1.0 is average and lower is better. Many utilities will not hire contractors above about 1.0, so a poor safety record can shut a contractor out of work.

The Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety rules, including those for power-line work and trenching. Employers log recordable injuries on the OSHA 300 log, the basis for TRIR.

The National Fire Protection Association's standard for electrical safety in the workplace, which governs arc-flash protection and who counts as a "qualified" electrical worker. Electrical testing technicians must be trained to it, which keeps them separate from general construction labor.

The International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, the main union for lineworkers, electricians and utility employees. Its outside-line branch supplies union line crews trained through joint apprenticeship programs run with the National Electrical Contractors Association (NECA).

aliases: Laborers' International Union of North America
Laborers International Union of North America
terms.definition: The Laborers' International Union of North America, which represents construction laborers, including many gas distribution and pipeline workers.

aliases: United Association of Journeymen and Apprentices of the Plumbing and Pipe Fitting Industry
terms.definition: The United Association of Journeymen and Apprentices of the Plumbing and Pipe Fitting Industry, the union for plumbers, pipefitters, welders and HVAC technicians, including pipeline welders.
The International Union of Operating Engineers, which represents heavy-equipment operators such as excavator, crane and drill-rig operators, as well as some stationary plant engineers.

A contractor whose workers are not covered by a union agreement. Union and open-shop contractors often serve different customers, and combining both in one company can create labor-relations limits on sharing crews.

A formal earn-while-you-learn program, registered with the Labor Department or a state, combining paid on-the-job work with classroom instruction. A lineworker apprenticeship takes about three to four years before the worker reaches "journeyman" status, which limits how fast skilled crews can be added.
A worker who builds and repairs overhead and underground power lines. BLS counts roughly 120,000 electrical power-line installers and repairers, among the scarcest and best-paid utility trades.

A commercial driver's license, required to drive heavy trucks such as hydrovacs, combination sewer cleaners and line trucks. CDL holders are in short supply and subject to federal drug and alcohol testing, which constrains how quickly crews can be staffed.

A 1931 federal law requiring contractors on federally funded construction to pay at least the locally "prevailing" wage and benefits, often set from union rates. It applies to IIJA and SRF-funded water projects, and many states have similar laws.

Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, a rough measure of operating cash profit. EBITDA margin is EBITDA as a share of revenue; "adjusted" EBITDA excludes items the company treats as one-off.

Enterprise value (the price of a company's equity plus its net debt) divided by EBITDA, the standard yardstick for pricing acquisitions. Small private service contractors often sell for roughly 4x to 7x EBITDA while large public utility service companies trade well into double digits, the gap a roll-up tries to capture.

A strategy, usually backed by private equity, of buying many small companies in a fragmented industry and combining them, aiming to sell the larger whole at a higher valuation multiple than was paid for the parts.
The first, usually larger, company a buyer acquires in a new sector, which supplies the management team, systems and customer base into which later add-ons are merged.
A smaller company bought by an existing platform company to add customers, territory, services or skilled crews. Add-ons are usually cheaper per dollar of EBITDA than platforms.

Profit from buying small companies at low valuation multiples and selling the combined, larger company at a higher one. For example, $10 million of EBITDA bought at 6x ($60 million) and later valued at 10x ($100 million) creates $40 million of value with no operating improvement.
Revenue growth from existing businesses, excluding revenue added by acquisitions. Investors value it more than acquired growth because it reflects real demand and market share gains.

The value of work a contractor has won but not yet performed. For utility MSAs it is an estimate of expected work orders over the contract term, so it is softer than a firm order book. Not to be confused with a replacement backlog of aging assets.
New contract awards in a period divided by revenue billed in the same period. A ratio above 1.0 means backlog is growing.
Cash tied up in running the business, mainly receivables and unbilled work minus payables. Service contractors are paid after doing the work, so fast growth absorbs cash even when profitable.
The average number of days a company takes to collect payment after billing. Utility contractors commonly run about 60 to 90 days, and slow-paying public customers push it higher.

Revenue minus direct job costs (crew labor, equipment, materials and subcontractors), as a share of revenue. Specialty testing and inspection services usually earn higher gross margins than heavy construction because skill, not equipment or materials, is the main input.

Selling, general and administrative expenses: overhead such as management, estimating, safety, IT and back office. In a roll-up, combining these functions across acquired companies is the most dependable source of margin improvement.
The degree to which profit grows faster than revenue because some costs, such as overhead, yard facilities and idle equipment, stay fixed as volume rises. It also works in reverse when volume falls.

Total addressable market: annual spending on the services a business could sell if it won every customer. The serviceable addressable market (SAM) is the narrower part it can realistically reach given its geography and capabilities.
Compound annual growth rate: the steady yearly growth rate that would take a value from its starting level to its ending level over a period.

A parent company that owns several operating businesses; here, the vehicle for owning services companies across business units. It can share capital, management and back-office functions while each unit keeps its own brand and crews.

An investment firm that buys companies using its funds' equity plus borrowed money, usually aiming to sell within about three to seven years. Companies a sponsor already owns are typically unavailable as platforms until the sponsor is ready to exit.

The share of revenue that comes from the largest customers. Small utility contractors often earn half or more from one or two utilities, so losing a single MSA renewal can be existential, and buyers price that in.

Revenue from work that repeats every year, such as mandated inspections, leak surveys, locating and maintenance under MSAs, as opposed to one-off projects. Buyers pay higher multiples for it because it is more predictable.

Private companies with roughly $10 million to $100 million of revenue, or a few million to about $15 million of EBITDA. Many are founder-owned, and they usually sell at lower multiples than larger companies.

The North American Industry Classification System, which assigns each business location a six-digit industry code based on its main activity. Federal counts of companies, payroll and jobs are organized by these codes, and a contractor doing several kinds of work is counted only under its main one.

Water and Sewer Line and Related Structures Construction: contractors building and repairing water mains, sewers, pumping stations and treatment plants. It is the federal industry code closest to the water business unit.

Oil and Gas Pipeline and Related Structures Construction: contractors building and repairing oil and gas pipelines, including gas distribution lines. It mixes large long-distance pipeline builders with local gas distribution contractors.

Power and Communication Line and Related Structures Construction: contractors building and maintaining power lines, substations and towers as well as telecom and cable lines. Many of its firms are telecom and fiber contractors, so not all serve electric utilities.

Electrical Contractors and Other Wiring Installation Contractors. It is dominated by building electricians but also holds many substation and electrical testing contractors, so it greatly overstates the utility testing niche.

Testing Laboratories and Services: firms that perform physical, chemical and other analytical testing, including some electrical, oil-testing and NDE companies. Like 238210, it is broad and only partly relevant.

A Census Bureau dataset counting firms, locations, jobs and payroll by industry code and by company size (number of employees), and every five years by revenue size. It is the best public source for how many small companies versus scaled players an industry has.

An annual Census Bureau dataset of business locations, jobs and payroll by industry code and by county, state or metro area. It shows where contractors are, but it counts locations rather than companies, so a firm with five branches appears five times.

The Census Bureau's survey of US businesses every five years (years ending in 2 and 7). It is the main federal source of revenue by detailed industry, including the value of construction work by type; the 2022 results are the latest benchmark.

Census Bureau counts of businesses with no paid employees, mostly self-employed individuals, by industry. They sit outside the main company counts and are not realistic acquisition targets, so including them inflates provider counts.

In Census data an establishment is a single business location, while a firm is all the locations under common ownership. Firm counts are the right measure of how many competitors exist; establishment counts run higher because larger companies have many branches.

The BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics survey, which estimates jobs and wages for about 800 occupations by industry and area. Comparing which occupations each industry employs is how this report tests whether crews overlap across business units.

The Standard Occupational Classification, the federal coding of jobs used in OEWS. Examples are 49-9051 (electrical power-line installers and repairers), 47-2152 (plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters) and 47-2073 (operating engineers and other construction equipment operators).

aliases: Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages
terms.definition: The BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages: near-complete counts of jobs, business locations and pay by industry and county, drawn from unemployment insurance records and published within about six months.

EIA's annual survey of every US power plant of 1 megawatt or more, listing each generator's technology, capacity, location and year it entered service. It is the source for how old the US power plant fleet is; the monthly version, EIA-860M, tracks planned additions and retirements.

EIA's annual survey of electric utilities covering customers, sales, revenue, ownership type, smart meters and reliability (SAIDI and SAIFI). It is the basis for counting utilities by type and for tracking grid reliability.

The annual financial report that major investor-owned electric utilities file with FERC, including plant in service and operation and maintenance expense by account, such as maintenance of overhead and underground lines. It lets outsiders measure what utilities actually spend on maintenance; FERC Form 2 is the equivalent for interstate gas pipelines.

The report every gas distribution utility files with PHMSA each year, listing miles of main and number of service lines by material, size and decade installed, plus leaks repaired by cause. It is the best public source for how old and leak-prone US gas pipe is.

aliases: Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey and Assessment
terms.definition: EPA's survey, every four years, of drinking-water systems' 20-year capital needs. The 7th DWINSA (2023) estimated $625 billion of needs and about 9.2 million lead service lines, and it is used to divide Drinking Water SRF money among states.

EPA's periodic survey of wastewater and stormwater capital needs. The 2022 survey, published in 2024, estimated about $630 billion of needs over 20 years, much of it for sewer pipes and overflow control.

synthesis.headline: The market is real and funded through utility rates, but this is a crowded, thin-margin roll-up category. Crews do not flex across gas, power and water, and margins do not grow with scale. FAM should start with one founder-owned gas maintenance platform bought at about 6-8x EBITDA, not a three-unit holding company.
synthesis.summary:
FAM's plan is a utility-infrastructure maintenance roll-up, a model others have run many times. The category is validated: Shermco (~$1.6B to Blackstone), Pike (>$5B EV reported), USIC, Osmose and Azuria/Inframark were profitable sponsor exits. The three-unit holding company is not validated. No one has built a scaled gas + power + water maintenance platform. The closest attempts failed (Williams, Orbital) or are distressed (Artera, the gas analogue).

The demand case holds for maintenance and replacement that utilities fund through their rates:
- investor-owned electric capex of ~$208B in 2025
- gas utility construction capex of $49.1B in 2023
- federally mandated gas inspection cycles
- 50-55% of distribution transformers older than 33 years
- water mains replaced on a ~125-year cycle
- nuclear plants licensed to 80 years

Population growth (+0.5%) and headline load growth are weak drivers, or mostly fund construction.

Three deck claims fail:
- '<10 scaled players' is false. There are 15-20, plus 26 sponsor-backed platforms.
- Crews do not flex across gas, power and water. Only ~15-27% of field headcount can move between units; the exception is gas-water at ~53% (est.).
- Margins do not expand with scale. MSA work earns 8-10% at any size.

The outsourced MRO market is ~$44-81B a year (est.). Recommended sequence:
- Start with one founder-owned gas distribution maintenance platform bought at ~6-8x EBITDA.
- Add water underground work in the same metros.
- Treat T&D as a later, separate company.
- Enter power-gen only through testing or inspection add-ons.

Underwrite 9-11% margins and cash yield, not multiple arbitrage.

answers.question: Is this basically an infrastructure maintenance roll-up? Who has built such platforms (competition), and which roll-ups are going well or badly (validation)?
answers.short_answer: Yes. It is a utility-infrastructure maintenance roll-up, and the category is proven by profitable exits (Shermco, Pike, USIC, Osmose, Azuria). The multi-unit holding company is not proven: the closest attempts failed or are distressed, and the field is crowded with at least 26 sponsor-backed platforms plus the public consolidators.
answers.answer:
Yes. Without the branding, this is a utility-infrastructure maintenance (MRO) roll-up, and the playbook has been run many times. The record validates the category, but not the three-unit design.

What has worked:
- Quanta, the 1990s roll-up: $28.48B FY2025 revenue at ~10.1% adj. EBITDA (Quanta 8-K). Scale bought labor depth and backlog, not premium margins.
- Shermco (NETA electrical testing): Blackstone agreed to pay ~$1.6B on Aug 21, 2025, after Shermco had bought regional NETA shops one at a time (Blackstone release).
- Pike (T&D): TPG Rise Climate took majority control in Dec 2025 at a reported >$5B EV including debt (Bloomberg, unconfirmed).
- United Utility Services: built by Bernhard from 2018 and sold for ~$1B including debt (Bloomberg via Energy Connects).
- USIC (locating, now on its third sponsor), Osmose (poles, EQT) and Azuria/Inframark (water, >$2.5B combined revenue, closed Apr 2026 per Inframark).
- Badger (hydrovac; builds its own trucks): 23.8% adj. EBITDA on $831.7M.

What has failed or struggled:
- Artera (CD&R) paid CenterPoint $850M in 2020 for Miller Pipeline and Minnesota Limited, which is in effect FAM's gas unit at scale. S&P cut it to CCC+ in Aug 2022 on leverage. Bloomberg Law reported >$2.5B of debt and that it had hired debt advisers.
- Williams Industrial (power-gen maintenance plus water) filed Chapter 11 in 2023 and sold for $60M after losing large contracts and losing money on water work (SEC filings).
- Orbital Infrastructure (T&D, telecom, renewables) filed Chapter 11 and liquidated in 2023. Charge Enterprises followed in 2024.
- Team Inc earned 2.7% adj. EBITDA in Q1 2025 and had to refinance; FY2025 was 6.8%.

Lessons:
1. Focus beats breadth. The best exits and margins come from one technically gated niche (Shermco, Badger, Osmose). Diversified holdcos are over-represented among the failures (Orbital, Williams), and nobody has built a scaled gas + power + water maintenance platform.
2. Debt plus utility buying power breaks roll-ups (Artera, Orbital). FAM's permanent, low-leverage capital is a genuine edge.
3. Fixed-price creep and customer concentration are the usual killers (Williams), which matches the deck's own avoid list.
4. Recurring is not the same as profitable. Centuri, the closest public analogue, earns 8.3% adj. EBITDA on $2.98B; Davey earns ~3.7% operating margin.

Competition is heavy. This research found 26 sponsor-backed platforms across the four sub-segments, owned by sponsors including Ridgemont, MPE, EQT, A&M, Kohlberg, Warren Equity, New Mountain, J.F. Lehman, Fort Point and CenterOak. The public consolidators (Quanta, MasTec, Primoris, MYR, Centuri, Dycom) compete too. Dycom paid 9.7x LTM EBITDA for Power Solutions (Delancey Street). FAM will bid against all of them for add-ons.

answers.question: Is there real employee and equipment utilization across business units, given the different equipment and expertise? Quantify.
answers.short_answer: Mostly no. Only about 15-27% of field headcount (est.) can move between gas or water and power, and those are the cheapest roles. Gas and water are the exception, at about 53% of headcount and 65% of fleet value. The real synergies are density, purchasing, insurance and back office, not crews flexing between units.
answers.answer:
Mostly no across units, yes within a unit, and partly between gas and water. Public labor data, credential rules and the way the closest comparables report all point the same way.

The labor pool (BLS OEWS, May 2023, NAICS 237100, ~576,000 workers implied):
- construction laborers: ~121,530 (~21%)
- power-line installers: 36,320 (6.3%)
- pipelayers: 13,770 (2.4%)
- boilermakers: 2,280 (0.4%)

More lineworkers work for utilities (57,100) than for contractors.

Estimated share of field headcount in roles that can actually move between units, built on the OEWS anchors. The movable roles are laborers, equipment operators and CDL drivers, plus electrical testers between T&D and power-gen.
- Gas-water: ~53%
- Gas-T&D and water-T&D: ~27%
- T&D-power-gen: ~25%
- Gas or water with power-gen: ~15%

Raw occupation overlap looks higher (39-83%), but it counts foremen and specialists who cannot cross. The movable roles are also the cheapest to hire. The scarce roles do not move:
- Lineworkers need a 7,000-hour (~3.5-year) apprenticeship (Washington L&I standards), and OSHA 1910.269 bars non-qualified crews from energized work.
- Gas operator qualification (PHMSA, 49 CFR 192 Subpart N) is specific to each utility, so crews face friction even between two gas customers.
- NETA Level III testers need ~5-8 years of experience (job postings, weak).
- Unions split by trade: UA/DCA for gas distribution, IBEW for line work, LIUNA for mainline pipe.

Equipment: the estimated share of fleet value usable by the other unit is:
- gas-water: ~65%
- gas-T&D: ~30%
- water-T&D: ~25%
- T&D-power-gen: ~20%
- power-gen with gas or water: ~10%

Pickups, excavators, dump trucks and vac trucks cross over. Insulated bucket trucks, digger derricks, wire pullers, leak-survey rigs, pipe-lining rigs and turbine tooling do not.

The comparables confirm it:
- Centuri reports four segments by trade and labor regime (U.S. Gas, Canadian Gas, Union Electric, Non-Union Electric), each with its own capex budget. Its storm revenue sits in electric, not gas (Centuri 10-K).
- National Grid keeps gas crews on standby during storms rather than using them on power lines.
- MYR does only 'limited gas construction'.
- A search of SEC filings found no company disclosing crew cross-utilization between gas and electric.

Where synergies are real (estimates, as a share of revenue):
- density and wallet share within a unit: 100-300 bps
- purchasing: 50-150 bps
- back office, safety and qualification records: 50-100 bps
- insurance: 30-100 bps
- shared fleet shops: 20-50 bps
- cross-unit crew flex: under 50 bps

The gas-water pairing is validated by Miller Pipeline (Artera), Hydromax and J.F. Kiely, which all do both.

Implication: build gas and water as one underground-pipe platform, and run T&D and power-gen as separate operating companies. Underwrite purchasing, overhead and density, not crew flex.

answers.question: Is infrastructure really aging, given routine maintenance? Is there a single US power line 50+ years old? Quantify like lead times.
answers.short_answer: Yes. Most of the US transmission grid dates from the 1960s-70s, and 50-55% of distribution transformers are older than 33 years. At today's replacement pace, clearing the old stock takes about 17-22 years for transformers, 11-16 years for gas cast iron, and a ~125-year cycle for water mains. Maintenance extends asset life, and that maintenance is the revenue, so aging is a slow, funded driver rather than a shock.
answers.answer:
Yes, and routine maintenance is why the thesis works, not a rebuttal of it. Maintenance stretches asset life, and that maintenance is the revenue. The deck, however, uses the weakest numbers available.

Is there a US power line over 50 years old? Yes, many:
- NASEO's grid primer says most of today's transmission grid dates to the 1960s-70s, which makes it roughly 46-66 years old now.
- The best-known case is PG&E's Caribou-Palermo 115 kV line. A worn C-hook on Tower 27/222 failed and started the 2018 Camp Fire (CAL FIRE; PG&E 8-K), and PG&E pleaded guilty to 84 counts of involuntary manslaughter. A secondary source dates the line to 1921; confirm that against the Butte County DA report before citing it.

Quantified like lead times, as years to clear the old stock at today's replacement pace:
- Distribution transformers (NREL for DOE): 60-80M units, 50-55% older than 33 years, with additions plus replacements of only 2.5-3% a year. Turning over the old half would take ~17-22 years even if every unit went to it.
- Large power transformers averaged 38-40 years in 2014, against a ~40-year design life (DOE).
- Wood poles: 130-160M are in service. Well maintained, they last 70-80+ years on ~10-year inspect-and-treat cycles, against a ~35-year book life (NAWPC). That is recurring inspection demand, not a replacement wave.
- Gas: PHMSA says 28% of distribution pipe was installed before 1970. Cast and wrought iron fell to ~16,337 miles in 2023, down 63% since 2005, and 24 states have finished. At 1,000-1,500 miles a year, it is gone in ~11-16 years. Bare steel (~61,000 miles around 2013) runs into the 2040s (UGI: 2041).
- Water: a 2023 Utah State survey of 802 utilities found 11.1 breaks per 100 miles a year (~260,000 breaks and $2.6B of repairs) and a $452B backlog of pipe past its useful life (ASCE). Mains are replaced on a ~125-year cycle (~0.8% a year) while the average pipe fails at ~53 years, so the backlog grows.
- Generation: coal units average 45 years and retire at ~50 (EIA), so that market shrinks. Nuclear is the opposite: the NRC renewed 18 licenses (~17 GW) in 15 months, many to 80 years.

Does spending follow? Grid Strategies/ACEG attributes ~90% of the $25B+ a year of transmission spend to reliability and replacement (not re-verified). Asset-condition projects are 73% of New England transmission owners' capital projects (Utility Dive).

Verdict: aging is real, measurable and funded through rate trackers, but it is slow and regional, not a shock. Replace the deck's 70%-of-the-grid figure with NREL's transformer data, and source the gas and water claims to PHMSA and Utah State.

answers.question: How many platform candidates exist per unit, based on the thesis criteria?
answers.short_answer: Few. Of 51 named candidates, 14 are platform-grade (gas 3, T&D 2, power-gen 5, water 4). Only 3 are confirmed independent, and 2 of those are unlikely sellers. The realistic list to pursue now is about 1-4 names plus a handful of gas regionals whose size still needs checking, so the real pipeline must come from primary contractor rosters.
answers.answer:
Few. We screened 85 named private companies against the thesis criteria: recurring maintenance, durable customers, specialized labor and equipment, safety, and no dependence on low-bid or fixed-price work. That left 51 candidates with their own websites. Of those, 14 are platform-grade (fit 4+, recurring, not bid-driven). Only 3 of the 14 are confirmed independent, and 2 of the 3 are unlikely sellers.

By unit:
- Gas: 14 listed, 3 platform-grade.
  - The three: Sparus/Southern Cross (Ridgemont since 2021), Heath Consultants (ownership unverified) and Artera (CD&R; too large).
  - Closest independent: Danella. It scores 3 because OSHA has investigated it six times since 2017 over trench work (NBC10).
  - Regional contractors Q3 Contracting, J.F. Kiely and Utility Line Services fit the model, but their size is unknown.
  - Add-ons: Teichert Pipelines, Pro-Vac/Hydromax, GPT, ULC Technologies.
- T&D: 12 listed, 2 platform-grade (Pike, owned by TPG; Osmose, owned by EQT), both sponsor-owned.
  - East Coast Power (A&M) and United Utility Services (Sandbrook/Blackstone) would add two more sponsored names.
  - No independent platform-grade company was found.
  - Vegetation managers (Asplundh, Davey, Lewis, Wright) score 3 because the work is thin-margin and re-bid.
- Power-gen, including NETA testing: 10 listed, 5 platform-grade.
  - The five: Day & Zimmermann (family), Structural Integrity Associates (employee-owned), Shermco (Blackstone), RESA Power (Kohlberg) and Allied Power Group (Warren Equity).
  - Only Day & Zimmermann and Structural Integrity are independent, and neither looks like a seller.
  - National Electric Coil is add-on scale.
- Water: 15 listed, 4 platform-grade.
  - The four: the Carylon group (family), Pittsburg Tank & Tower and Maguire Iron (ownership unverified), and USG Water Solutions (sponsor-owned).
  - Water has the most independent candidates. They cluster in tank asset-management contracts (fixed annual fee, provider carries the maintenance risk) and in annual sewer cleaning and CCTV programs.
  - Spiniello and SAK fail the low-bid screen.
  - Lead-line and meter installers do low-bid subcontract work. For example, Watertown awarded $7.77M to the low bidder.

Realistic list to pursue now: about 1-4 names, plus 3-6 gas regionals if their size checks out.

Why so few:
- 26 sponsor-backed platforms already hold most of the scaled assets.
- Much line, lead-pipe and meter work is bought by low bid.
- Web search under-represents founder-owned $10-50M firms, which is where FAM's platform would come from.

The gas universe is bounded. The Distribution Contractors Association has ~240 member companies, including suppliers.

Next step: build the list from primary rosters: DCA, NETA accredited companies, NASSCO, AWWA, state PUC and utility contractor prequalification lists, and co-op vendor lists. Read a fit score of 3 with mostly unknown fields as not yet diligenced, not as weak.

answers.question: Is the 'why now' sufficient: nuclear and solar, is population really growing, is power demand actually rising despite efficiency?
answers.short_answer: Not as written. Population growth has slowed to 0.5%, and load growth is real but driven by data centers and mostly funds construction. The defensible why-now is record replacement capex that utilities recover through their rates, mandated gas compliance cycles, and asset life extension, especially nuclear to 80 years. The headwinds the deck omits are a withdrawn PHMSA leak rule, the end of IIJA water money and pending litigation over the lead-pipe rule.
answers.answer:
Not as written. The deck leans on drivers that mostly fund new construction, which FAM excludes, and on population, which is barely growing. A stronger why-now exists.

Population: drop it.
- Census Vintage 2025 shows +0.5% growth to 341.8M, the slowest since 2021.
- Net international migration fell from 2.7M (2024) to 1.3M (2025), and ~321k is projected for 2026.
- What growth there is sits in the Sun Belt and means new connections, which is construction.

Power demand: the instinct is right for homes and wrong for the total.
- Efficiency is real: residential use per customer fell 2.3% from 2009 to 2019 (EIA), and total use was flat in 2015-2021 at ~3.86-4.0 trillion kWh.
- Use then hit a record 4,195 BkWh in 2025. EIA's Oct 2026 STEO forecasts 4,288 for 2026 and 4,356 for 2027, led by commercial load (data centers).
- LBNL puts data centers at 176 TWh in 2023 (4.4% of US use) and 325-580 TWh by 2028.
- Grid Strategies' 5-year peak forecast rose from 24 GW to 166 GW in three years, though it flags ~25 GW of data-center double counting.
- Growth is concentrated in ERCOT and PJM and mostly pays for generation, transmission and interconnection builds.

Nuclear: the clearest maintenance signal.
- The NRC renewed 18 licenses (~17 GW) in 15 months, including 80-year approvals for Turkey Point, Surry, Browns Ferry, St. Lucie and Hatch.
- Restarts add ~2.25 GW (Palisades ~Mar 2027; Crane 2027). SMRs are post-2030 construction.
- Outage work requires NRC Appendix B quality programs and is held by incumbents.

Solar, wind and storage: a record 53 GW was added in 2025 and 86 GW is planned for 2026 (EIA). The O&M pool (est. $7-10B) goes largely to equipment makers and owners, and the OBBBA tax-credit phase-out points to a 2026-27 peak.

What should anchor the why-now:
- Replacement capex that utilities recover through their rates. EEI members' capex rose from $139.8B (2020) to ~$207.9B (2025E), with >$1.1T planned for 2025-29. Gas utility construction capex rose from $32.7B to $49.1B in 2022-23 (AGA).
- Mandated recurring work: 49 CFR 192 leak surveys, cathodic protection and regulator inspections.
- Life extension: nuclear to 80 years, poles to 70-80+.

Headwinds the deck omits:
- PHMSA's leak-detection rule was withdrawn in Jan 2025; a new proposal has sat at DOT since Apr 30, 2026.
- FY2026 was the last year of IIJA supplemental SRF money ($2,603M per fund).
- The Nov 2027 lead-line deadline is in litigation.
- Affordability pressure is rising.

Utilities earn a return on capex but not on O&M, so FAM should target the replacement programs utilities capitalize.

answers.question: What is the TAM? What revenue could the platform reach, at what margins, and how do economics improve with scale?
answers.short_answer: The outsourced maintenance market is about $44-81B a year (est.): T&D $20-35B, gas $12-20B, water $8-18B, power-gen $4-8B. A realistic FAM platform is about $50M of revenue at entry, built to about $150M through add-ons, at a 9-11% EBITDA margin. Scale adds roughly 0-1 point of margin; most of the scale benefit is a higher valuation multiple, which a permanent-capital owner does not cash unless it sells or recapitalizes.
answers.answer:
The deck has no TAM and no margin case. The market is big enough; the margin story is not.

TAM, outsourced MRO only (the spend pools are sourced; the outsourced shares are estimates):
- Gas: $12-20B a year (35-55% of AGA's $33-37B annual safety spend).
- T&D: $20-35B. This is the replacement and hardening share of $50.9B distribution and $32.6B transmission capex, plus outsourced vegetation, inspection, testing and storm work.
- Power-gen maintenance: $4-8B of ~$13B of plant maintenance (EIA cost per MWh x generation), after OEM service agreements and in-house work. It is shrinking with coal.
- Water: $8-18B (CBO: $113B of public water spending in 2017, $82B of it O&M that is mostly done in-house).
- Total: ~$44-81B. A $500M holdco would hold ~1%.

Margins (FY2025 adj. EBITDA):
- Quanta 10.1%, Mistras 12.6%, Centuri 8.3%, MasTec 8.0%
- Primoris ~6.9%, Team 6.8%, ESOA 4.2%, Badger 23.8%

Specialty and asset-heavy niches earn 12-24%; MSA labor work earns 8-10%. Scale alone adds roughly 0-2 points. Fixed-price problems swing margins hard: MYR's gross margin moved from 8.6% to 11.6%, and MasTec Pipeline's from 18.3% to 14.9%.

Revenue and margin path (illustrative estimate; 70% MSA field work, 30% specialty testing):
- $50M platform: ~11.0% EBITDA ($5.5M), often helped by owner add-backs.
- $150M: ~9.5% ($14M), because holdco safety, finance and ERP costs land before the synergies do.
- $500M: ~11.3% ($56.5M), with a range of 9-13%.

Bridge from $50M to $500M:
- holdco cost: -1.2 pts
- integration: -0.7
- procurement: +0.4 (utilities often supply the major materials)
- equipment: +0.4
- insurance and benefits: +0.4
- SG&A leverage: +1.0

The net is ~+0.3 pts. Underwrite 9-11% at steady state.

Where scale does help:
- Multiples. Lower-middle-market deals cleared at 6.4x ($10-25M TEV), 6.8x ($25-50M) and 8.3x ($50-100M) in 9M 2025 (GF Data, all industries). Scaled assets sit at 11-16x: Centuri's IPO was ~11-12x (est.) and it trades at 12-16x, the public peer median is 15.2x, and Qualus paid 14.9x.
- For permanent capital, that multiple gap is a mark, not cash, unless FAM recapitalizes or sells. The cash case must stand on its own. At a 7x entry and an 11% margin, EBITDA less 3-4% fleet capex is ~9.7% of the purchase price a year, pre-tax and before organic growth (est.).
- Risk costs fall with size: insurance pooling, safety programs and fleet buying all improve.

Expectation: buy a ~$50M founder-owned platform at ~6-8x, build it to ~$150M through add-ons, and earn 9-11%. $500M is a long-horizon outcome, not a plan.

key_numbers.label: Pre-tax cash yield at 7x entry, 11% margin, 3-4% fleet capex

answers.question: Verify '20,000+ providers' and '<10 scaled players' with real numbers and named companies.
answers.short_answer: '20,000+' is roughly right. The Census counted 18,877 utility-system construction firms in 2017, down from 25,227 in 2012, but the relevant pool is much smaller (e.g. ~240 gas distribution contractor members of DCA). '<10 scaled players' is false: 15-20 named players have revenue around or above $1B, though fewer than 10 operate in each sub-segment and none spans gas, power and water at scale.
answers.answer:
The deck's '20,000+ providers' is roughly right but measures the wrong thing. Its '<10 meaningful scaled players' is false.

Firm count:
- The 2017 Economic Census counted 18,877 utility-system construction businesses (NAICS 2371) with 570,952 employees (NUCA 2026 fact sheet). The 2012 census counted 25,227, so the count fell ~25% in five years.
- VerticalIQ models ~17,800 firms and ~$158B of revenue.
- Six-digit counts from aggregators conflict badly (237130: 2,773 vs 7,112 vs 13,809), so don't cite them.
- NAICS 2371 includes new construction and telecom. Adding electrical contractors and repair firms would push the total past 20,000.

The relevant pool is far smaller:
- The Distribution Contractors Association, the trade group for gas distribution contractors, has ~240 member companies, including suppliers.
- Firm size is skewed. In 2005, 3.2% of pipeline-construction firms had 500+ employees and held 52.8% of the jobs (Census SUSB).
- Our estimate: ~100-400 firms in 2371 have 500+ staff, and platform-quality maintenance firms number in the low hundreds.

Scaled players with largely US utility and energy infrastructure revenue (website, revenue):
- Quanta, quantaservices.com: $28.48B
- MasTec, mastec.com: $14.3B
- Primoris, prim.com: ~$7.6B
- Asplundh, asplundh.com: ~$4.7-6.3B (weak sourcing)
- MYR Group, myrgroup.com: $3.66B
- Centuri, centuri.com: $2.98B
- Artera, artera.com: >$2.6B
- Azuria/Inframark, azuria.com: >$2.5B
- Davey Tree, davey.com: ~$1.95B
- Pike, pike.com: $1.7B in 2020, roughly doubled since (Lindsay Goldberg)
- Day & Zimmermann, dayzim.com: #1 power O&M contractor (ENR 2023)
- Michels, michels.us: ENR Top 400 #38

Next tier:
- Shermco, shermco.com: ~$1.6B deal value
- Team, teaminc.com: $896.5M
- Badger, badgerinc.com: $831.7M
- Mistras, mistrasgroup.com: $724.0M
- USIC (usicllc.com) and Osmose (osmose.com): revenue undisclosed

That is 15-20 scaled players.

By sub-segment, the deck's framing fits better:
- gas: ~6 scaled players
- power-gen maintenance: 2-4 independents
- T&D: 8+
- water: essentially one >$1B player

The top is concentrated. Quanta plus MasTec equal ~27% of the $158B pool. That ratio is rough, because their revenue includes non-US and renewables work.

Defensible rewrite: '~19,000 utility-system contractors (Census 2017), mostly small; 15-20 players with revenue around or above $1B; fewer than 10 in each sub-segment; none spanning gas, power and water at scale.'

deck_claims.claim: 25% of US natural gas distribution mains are more than 50 years old
deck_claims.better_statement: PHMSA (2021) reports that 28% of the US gas distribution system was installed before 1970, so that pipe is now 56+ years old. PHMSA-cited data count about 423K miles of pre-1970 mains out of about 1.3M miles, including about 87K miles of unknown vintage. The riskiest material, cast and wrought iron, is down to about 1% of mains (about 16K miles) and is being retired at about 1,000 miles a year. Most of the remaining work is in 1950s-70s bare steel and early plastic, not cast iron. Re-pull the CY2024 by-decade inventory before publishing.

deck_claims.claim: 70% of the US electric grid is over 25 years old
deck_claims.better_statement: DOE (2022) says more than 70% of transmission lines and power transformers are over 25 years old. The statistic dates back to at least 2006, it does not cover the whole grid, and 25 years is well inside a 40-60+ year design life. A stronger, current figure is NREL's: about 50-55% of the 60-80M US distribution transformers are older than 33 years, and only 2.5-3% of units are added or replaced each year.

deck_claims.claim: Some US water infrastructure is now more than a century old
deck_claims.better_statement: The claim is true but unquantified. A 2023 Utah State survey of 802 utilities found 11.1 main breaks per 100 miles per year, about 260,000 breaks and $2.6B of repairs annually, and $452B of pipe past its useful life. Mains are replaced on a ~125-year cycle against an average failure age of ~53 years. In Philadelphia, about 15% of mains were laid before 1900.

deck_claims.claim: $625B drinking water infrastructure investment need over 20 years
deck_claims.better_statement: EPA's 7th DWINSA (2021 survey data, released 2023) puts the 20-year drinking-water need at $625B, up 32% from $472.6B, with $420.8B for transmission and distribution. It is a needs estimate, not funded spending. FY2026 was the last year of IIJA supplemental SRF money, and EPA's Nov 2025 update cut the lead-service-line estimate to about 4M from 9.2M.

The Census counted 18,877 utility-system construction businesses (NAICS 2371) with 570,952 employees in 2017, down from 25,227 in 2012. That count includes new construction and telecom. The relevant pool is far smaller: the gas distribution contractors' trade group (DCA) has ~240 members, and platform-quality maintenance firms number in the low hundreds (est.). Say: about 19,000 utility-system contractors (Census), mostly small.

At least 15-20 scaled public or sponsor-backed consolidators operate across these sub-segments. They include Quanta ($28.5B), MasTec ($14.3B), Primoris (~$7.6B), Asplundh, MYR ($3.7B), Centuri ($3.0B), Artera (>$2.6B), Azuria/Inframark (>$2.5B), Davey (~$1.95B), Pike (>$5B EV reported), Day & Zimmermann, Michels, Shermco (~$1.6B deal), Badger, Mistras and Team. On top of these, 26 sponsor-backed platforms are buying add-ons. The claim holds only per sub-segment, and no one spans gas, power and water at scale.

deck_claims.claim: Employee and equipment utilization across units: crews flex across segments and specialized assets move across jobs and regions
deck_claims.better_statement:
Credentials and unions keep crafts apart:
- Lineworkers need ~7,000-hour apprenticeships and OSHA 1910.269 qualification.
- Gas crews need PHMSA operator qualifications that are specific to each utility.
- Unions split by trade: UA/DCA for gas, IBEW for line work.
- Centuri reports its segments by trade and labor regime.

An estimated ~15-27% of field headcount and ~10-30% of fleet value can move between gas or water and power. Gas and water underground work is the exception, at about 53% of headcount and 65% of fleet value (est.). Specialized assets do move across regions within one unit, as storm mobilization shows.

deck_claims.claim: Wallet share, shared branch overhead, material and equipment purchases, insurance and benefits
deck_claims.better_statement:
These synergies are real but modest. Estimated as a share of revenue:
- density and wallet share within a unit: 100-300 bps
- purchasing: 50-150 bps
- back office and safety: 50-100 bps
- insurance: 30-100 bps
- shared fleet shops: 20-50 bps

Utilities often supply the major materials, and workers' comp is priced by trade class. Holdco costs (~1.2-2% of revenue) and integration (~0.7 pts) offset much of the gain, so underwrite a net margin gain of only ~0-1 point (est.).

unit_ranking.why:
Best first platform, for four reasons.
- Work is mandated and recurring under 49 CFR 192: annual leak surveys in business districts, annual cathodic protection checks, rectifier checks six times a year and annual regulator-station inspections.
- Replacement is funded through state rate trackers, with bare steel running to ~2041 at UGI.
- The target universe is bounded and knowable: ~240 DCA members.
- It is the only unit with a real labor and fleet link to another unit. With water it shares ~53% of movable headcount and ~65% of fleet value (est.). It also ties into Imperial (meter brass, service and cable scrap), Transend (pipe freight) and Panther (fittings).

Risks:
- Artera, the same unit at scale, is distressed.
- Centuri earns only 8.3%.
- Cast iron is finite (~16K miles left).
- The PHMSA leak rule was withdrawn.
- Compliance contracts are often re-bid on unit price.

fam_plan.first_unit: Natural gas distribution maintenance, built as an underground-utility platform that later adds water and wastewater work in the same metros
fam_plan.rationale:
Gas distribution maintenance is the only unit that combines four advantages:
1. Recurring work that is mandated on a calendar (49 CFR 192 leak surveys, cathodic protection, regulator inspections), plus replacement programs funded through state rate trackers.
2. A bounded target universe (~240 DCA members) that still includes founder-owned regional firms not held by sponsors.
3. The one real cross-unit synergy: gas shares crews and fleet with water underground work (~53% of movable headcount, ~65% of fleet value, est.).
4. The most direct links to FAM's metals, fittings and freight businesses.

It also carries the clearest warning. Artera, the same unit built at scale with heavy debt, is distressed, and Centuri earns 8.3%. FAM's edge is to buy small, at ~6-8x, with low leverage and no forced exit.

T&D is larger but picked over. Power-gen is small and dominated by OEM service arms.
steps: Nov 2026: Rewrite the deck with the edits listed below and narrow unit 1 to gas distribution MRO. Adopt these screens: ~6-8x EBITDA entry; at least two utility MSA customers; most revenue from MSA or unit-rate maintenance (not fixed-price or one-off low-bid work); a clean OSHA and EMR record; and leverage far below the level that broke Artera.

Nov-Dec 2026: Build a primary-source list of 40-60 founder- or family-owned gas contractors with $20-100M of revenue. Sources: the DCA directory (~240 members), state PUC filings on utility replacement programs (NJ, NY, MA, PA and MI hold the most remaining cast iron) and utility contractor prequalification lists.

Dec 2026: Approach the named independents first: Heath Consultants once its ownership is confirmed, and Q3 Contracting, J.F. Kiely and Utility Line Services once their size is confirmed. Treat Danella as conditional on passing a safety screen. Skip sponsor auctions priced above the screen.

Q1 2027: Diligence each platform candidate on MSA terms and renewal dates, customer tenure, revenue mix by work type, PHMSA operator-qualification records, union status (UA/DCA vs non-union), and equipment ownership and fleet age. Target one LOI by the end of Q1 2027 for a ~$50M-revenue platform (illustratively ~$5.5M EBITDA, ~$37-46M EV at 6.8-8.3x).

2027: Make the first add-ons inside the platform's existing utility territories: leak survey, cathodic protection and regulator-station maintenance (all mandated under 49 CFR 192), plus hydro-excavation. The goal is density (est. 100-300 bps) and a larger share of each utility's spend.
2027: Set up a lean holdco covering safety, operator-qualification records, insurance and fleet purchasing. Budget ~1-2% of revenue for it, and plan for a margin dip around $150M of revenue.

2027, after the D.C. Circuit rules on LCRI: Add water underground work in the same metros. Take lead service lines only under negotiated or unit-rate programs. Also add sewer cleaning and CCTV, and tank asset management (Carylon, Pittsburg Tank & Tower or Maguire, after ownership checks).

Nov 2026-2027: Run the portfolio links as small pilots. Imperial quotes buybacks of meter brass, service-line and cable scrap from the platform and its utility customers. Transend quotes pipe freight. Panther and SFE quote fittings and specialty castings. Spend no capex without purchase orders.

2028 and later: Revisit T&D as a separate operating company only if a lower-middle-market distribution-maintenance or substation-testing firm is available within the screen. Enter power-gen only through NETA or NDE add-ons.
Review gates: in Jan 2027, decide go or no-go on the target list. In mid-2027, commit to or stop the first platform. Each year after, re-underwrite against the watchlist and signals.

risks.risk: Overpaying in a sponsor-crowded market (Pike >$5B reported, Shermco ~$1.6B, public peers at ~15.2x)
risks.mitigation: Buy founder- and family-owned firms at ~6-8x. Skip auctions priced above the screen. Build the pipeline from primary rosters, not banker books.

risks.risk: Thin margins that do not expand with scale (MSA work earns 8-10%; ~+0.3 pts net from $50M to $500M, est.)
risks.mitigation: Underwrite 9-11% steady-state margins and cash yield. Give no credit for cross-unit crew flex. Keep holdco costs to ~1-2% of revenue.

risks.risk: Leverage meeting utility buying power, as at Artera (>$2.5B of debt) and Orbital
risks.mitigation: Use permanent capital with modest leverage (Centuri deleveraged to 2.5x), stagger maturities, and avoid one large transformative deal.

risks.risk: Creep into fixed-price and low-bid work (Williams; margin swings at MYR and MasTec Pipeline)
risks.mitigation: Cap fixed-price and low-bid revenue in the platform criteria. Buy add-ons whose work is MSA or unit-rate. Report job-level margins from day one.

risks.risk: Customer concentration and loss of an MSA (Williams lost large contracts in 2022)
risks.mitigation: Require at least two utility MSAs at entry. Diligence renewal dates and tenure. Expand with existing customers before entering new geographies.

risks.risk: Finite replacement programs: cast iron is ~16K miles, ~11-16 years from done
risks.mitigation: Target bare steel, vintage plastic, service lines and mandated compliance work, which run into the 2040s.

risks.risk: Regulatory and funding timing: PHMSA leak rule withdrawn, LCRI in litigation, IIJA SRF money ended in FY2026
risks.mitigation: Build the base case on existing state rate-tracker programs only. Treat federal rules and federal money as upside.

risks.risk: Safety and qualification exposure (OSHA trench cases; gas operator qualifications specific to each utility)
risks.mitigation: Screen OSHA history and EMR. Centralize operator-qualification records and the safety program at the holdco. Walk away from repeat trench citations.

risks.risk: Labor scarcity and split union jurisdictions (UA/DCA, IBEW, LIUNA)
risks.mitigation: Map union status for each target. Do not assume crews can move between units or regions. Budget ~0.7 pts for wage harmonization.

risks.risk: Affordability pressure on utility rates and O&M budgets
risks.mitigation: Favor replacement programs that utilities capitalize and earn a return on over O&M work they expense.
